Mr. Speaker, in spite of all that has been said in this rather lengthy debate there are still a few points which I think should be emphasized if we are going to face this problem honestly and squarely, and if we are going to give our people a true picture not only of the causes of unemployment but also of what can and what cannot be done about it.
We are all concerned about the steady growth of unemployment during the past three years and the serious proportions it has now attained-a situation which is all the more serious because it has occurred during a period of expanding economy and general prosperity. We all appreciate what this means to the unemployed in terms of human misery, suffering, privation and agony of mind and spirit, as well as the moral disintegration which so often results. Our human resources are the most precious of all our resources, and our humanitarian instincts demand that no stone be left unturned to' solve this problem and prevent its recurrence.
When I consider this problem I cannot help thinking about the thousands of fishermen and their dependents in my own riding who,, although they are not included in the unemployment totals, are nevertheless out of work due to the seasonal nature of their occupation and who find themselves forced to endure the same conditions as the jobless elsewhere. In many cases their position is even worse because they have toiled all year for little or nothing, and do not even enjoy the benefits of unemployment insurance.
What makes this unemployment problem so difficult is the fact that there are so many contributing factors and it is impossible to-

measure the influence of any of them with any degree of accuracy. To explain it by saying that our labour force has expanded faster than our economy is in my opinion an oversimplification. Unemployment is the result of many forces, all of different strength and direction and all interrelated, interreacting one upon the other to produce a sort of chain reaction of higher costs, decreased exports, lower farm income, reduced retail sales and unemployment.
We have learned from the speeches made by the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Trade and Commerce that these forces can be classified under four main headings. First, there are the forces of nature, of climate and geography which practically control our seasonal industries and affect even industries like the construction industry. These cause great fluctuations in seasonal and regional employment. There are also the vagaries of weather, of frost and drought, which along with plant diseases and insect plagues produce a serious effect upon the agricultural component of our gross national product.
Second, there are industrial forces which are at work inside the industry itself. Foremost among these are labour-management relations, because strikes contribute to unemployment in supplementary industries which manufacture parts and accessories. Under this heading we must also include the forces of technological progress, such as more efficient machines and improved methods and processes. Being squeezed between the pressure of higher costs of labour and materials on the one side, and the pressure of foreign competition and consumer sales resistance on the other, management is compelled to find ways and means of increasing output without increasing the number of jobs.
In the long run this turns out to be a good thing because greater efficiency and a stronger competitive position make possible expansion which provides more jobs later on, but during the transitional period this expansion has to be paid for by an increase in unemployment.
Third, we have the economic forces which fall into two groups. The first group constitutes the external or foreign forces, while the second group is made up of the internal or domestic forces.
Among the external forces we include the trend of foreign trade, the fiscal policies of the countries which constitute our most important markets, and the upward or downward trend of their economies. The fiscal policies of these countries include tariffs,
Unemployment
quotas, currency regulations, convertibility and restrictions against dollar goods.
Among the internal forces we have our own trade policies, domestic and foreign; our fiscal policies in the form of tariff protection; the availability of credit and money; tax policies; public investment, encouragement to private capital and investment; subsidies and subventions to industries; price supports and assistance to consumer purchasing power through social security payments.
Finally, we have what might be described as human forces. We have mentioned already labour-management relations under the heading of industrial forces, but we must not forget the forces of greed, selfishness and comparative honesty which affect the unemployment situation to a far greater degree than many of us perhaps realize.
I have enumerated all these forces, Mr. Speaker, for three reasons. My first reason is to show how difficult and complicated the problem is, and to emphasize the fact that because of these complications no simple, easy or quick solution is possible.
My second reason is to point out that of all the numerous forces which tend to create unemployment, only a few can be controlled or influenced by the federal government or indeed by any other level of government, be it provincial or municipal.
My third reason is to emphasize that we must be extremely careful not to mislead the public into thinking that there is any quick or simple solution to this problem, or that any rapid improvement would occur as the result of calling a federal-provincial conference. That is not to say that a conference would not be useful; indeed, it would be well worth while if it did nothing more than define and clarify the different spheres and levels of responsibility. If it succeeded in creating teamwork that would result in a commitment to joint action and co-operation in attacking the problem, then so much the better.
It should be clearly explained to the public that the majority of the forces which tend to create unemployment fall outside the influence or control of the federal parliament or of the provincial and municipal governments. Let us consider me forces of nature, for example. What can any level of government do about nature, the vagaries of the weather or its effect upon the amount of grain or butter which will become a part of our gross national product?
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) called attention to the fact that unemployment and a decrease in farm income always occur simultaneously, and he

Unemployment
suggested that the former was a direct result of the latter. I do not think this point can be proved. I feel it is far more logical to assume that both unemployment and lower farm income are the direct results of other factors. Furthermore, if the cure is to increase farm income there is a limit to what the federal government can do in this regard, because the federal government is limited by What the taxpayer is prepared to pay and also by the competitive position of Canada in the foreign market. The government is already doing what it can to protect farmers against these contingencies and to help stabilize their purchasing power.
In addition to what has already been done to accomplish this, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) has made some constructive suggestions to encourage the construction industry to expand its winter operations. Although he referred particularly to housing I think his suggestion could also be applied to the shipbuilding industry, and possibly to the construction of public buildings and even hospitals and schools,
Let us consider the industrial forces. What control has the government over technological progress, wage disputes, strikes, etc.? Both the federal and provincial governments are doing an excellent job in the field of labour-management relations, and it is difficult to see what more can be expected.
Let us also consider the economic forces. What control has the federal government over the economy of the United States or of the United Kingdom or of any other country which
constitutes an important market for Canadian goods? What control do we have over the foreign tariffs, the currency restrictions or the foreign competition of those countries?
As far as the internal economic forces are concerned the government does have some measure of control. In fact this is the only sphere where the federal government can exert direct influence to any great extent; but even in this field their ability to exert influence is often limited by outside forces. In this respect the government can be compared to the operator of a control panel. The government turns one dial here and another dial there in an effort to keep our internal economic forces in balance with each other. At the same time these internal forces must be prevented from getting out of balance with the external forces, so that our Canadian economy can always be easily adjusted to changing influences.
